title: Tata Motors Is Ramping EV Production by 50% — and Turning to China's Chery to Build Its Premium Electric Future
excerpt: With EV bookings surging 2.5 times on rising fuel costs, Tata is scaling output from 10,000 to 15,000 units a month while licensing Chery's Freelander platform for its delayed Avinya luxury EVs — a strategy that blends domestic manufacturing ambition with quiet Chinese technology dependence.
body:
Something unexpected is happening in India's car market. Electric vehicle bookings at Tata Motors — the country's dominant EV maker — have surged 2 to 2.5 times in two months, driven not by government subsidies or green idealism but by the oldest economic motivator there is: fuel prices.

With petrol and diesel costs elevated by lingering geopolitical tensions from the West Asia conflict, Indian buyers are doing the maths and concluding that an electric car is no longer a lifestyle statement. It is a hedge. At Tata Motors, EVs now account for nearly 30 percent of all bookings, up from roughly 12 to 14 percent of sales just months ago. In May 2026, the company delivered 10,517 EVs — an 85 percent year-on-year increase and a new monthly record.

"People want at least one electric car in their garage," Shailesh Chandra, the managing director of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, told reporters. "The momentum has intensified further in the last few weeks."

## The Production Bottleneck

The demand surge has exposed a constraint that Tata is now racing to fix: it cannot build EVs fast enough. Current production runs at about 10,000 units a month, and the company is planning a 50 percent ramp-up to 15,000 within three to four months.

The bottleneck is not inside Tata's own factories. Internal capacity is adequate. The constraint sits with suppliers — the vendors who produce EV-specific batteries, power electronics, and specialised components. Chandra was candid about the gap: "If I was able to supply, my market share would have stepped up a bit. But my market share is defined by the supply."

The company is investing heavily to close this gap. Tata has committed ₹160 to 180 billion (roughly $1.9 to $2.1 billion) in its EV business between FY25 and FY30, covering dedicated EV architectures, manufacturing upgrades, and product development. A brownfield expansion at the Sanand facility in Gujarat will add 300,000 units of annual capacity over the next few years.

If the production ramp succeeds, Tata could cross the milestone of 100,000 EVs in a single financial year — a number that would make India's EV transition look less like a pilot project and more like an industrial shift.

## The Chery Play: Chinese Tech Under the Tata Badge

While scaling up its mass-market EVs, Tata is also executing a strategic pivot at the premium end — one that involves a quiet but significant reliance on Chinese technology.

Reuters reported in early June that Tata Motors will license an automaking platform from China's Chery Automobile for its premium Avinya electric brand. The platform comes through the Chery-JLR Freelander joint venture, and the first Avinya model is expected to launch in 2027, assembled at Tata's newly opened factory in Panapakkam, Tamil Nadu.

This is a reset. Tata had originally planned to build Avinya on Jaguar Land Rover's Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA), a plan announced in 2023 and initially targeted for 2025. That roadmap collapsed when JLR shelved its Indian EV platform ambitions, forcing Tata into what one industry source called "a stop-gap arrangement."

The Chery platform deal compensates for the lost time, giving Tata access to advanced EV features and engineering that it would otherwise take years and significantly more capital to develop in-house. The first Avinya on Chery's platform will arrive as a kit from China and be assembled locally, with localisation efforts already underway. A second model is planned for 2029, with the possibility of two more beyond that.

Tata has been careful with the messaging. The company said in a statement that Chery "will act as a supplier of platforms to be used for Avinya" and added that "there is no licensing or technology transfer being done." But the practical reality is clear: India's largest EV maker is building its premium electric future on a Chinese foundation.

## The Broader India EV Picture

The Tata story is emblematic of India's EV market in 2026. The country's overall EV penetration remains low — roughly 5.5 to 6 percent of new passenger vehicle sales — but the trajectory has steepened. If supply constraints ease, Chandra estimates penetration could reach 8 to 10 percent relatively quickly.

Three forces are converging:

**Fuel economics**: The West Asia conflict pushed crude oil above $80 a barrel for extended periods, making the running-cost case for EVs undeniable. Even with Brent now retreating toward $72 on the back of US-Iran peace talks and reopened Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes, petrol prices in India remain elevated due to tax structures and refining margins.

**Affordability**: Tata has aggressively lowered the entry point. The refreshed Tiago EV starts at ₹4.69 lakh (about $5,500), with a lifetime battery warranty. Based on usage data from 75,000 existing Tiago EV owners who have collectively driven two billion kilometres, Tata calculates that a typical owner clocking 1,500 km a month would recover the full vehicle cost through fuel savings within four to five years. "After that point, the car starts paying you," Chandra said.

**Competitive pressure**: Mahindra & Mahindra, JSW MG Motor, and Maruti Suzuki are all expanding their EV lineups, narrowing Tata's first-mover advantage. The Chery platform deal for Avinya is partly a defensive move to plug gaps in the premium segment before competitors fill them.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

Tata Motors stock (NSE: TATAMOTORS) is one of the most widely held Indian equities among diaspora investors, both directly and through mutual funds and ETFs that track the Nifty Auto index. The EV transition creates a two-sided investment thesis.

**The bull case** is clear: Tata has a commanding 60-plus percent share of India's passenger EV market, demand is accelerating faster than expected, the Punch EV and Nexon EV are proven mass-market winners, and the company is backed by $1 billion from TPG and PLI (Production Linked Incentive) scheme benefits potentially worth $750 million.

**The bear case** centres on margin pressure — Chandra acknowledged that Tata is "sacrificing margins to some extent" on EVs — and the growing reliance on Chinese technology at a time when New Delhi is pushing supply-chain self-reliance. The Chery partnership, while commercially pragmatic, introduces geopolitical risk. India's restrictions on Chinese investment remain in place, and any escalation in Sino-Indian tensions could complicate the Avinya supply chain.

The stock is also a proxy for India's broader manufacturing story. If EV adoption accelerates, Tata's ancillary businesses — Tata Chemicals (battery materials), Tata Power (EV charging), and the new Agratas gigafactory — stand to benefit. If adoption stalls due to infrastructure gaps or consumer resistance, the entire thesis is delayed.

For NRI investors weighing the Indian auto sector, the question is not whether India will go electric. It will. The question is whether Tata can build fast enough, localise fast enough, and manage its Chinese supply-chain dependencies carefully enough to maintain its lead as the field gets crowded.
